pll1d31c2-d1e3501.summary: Introduces Hilary's assignment of properties, 'eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift,' so difficult that Augustine labored over it. Augustine thinks 'eternity' means only that the Father has no father from whom he is, while the Son is from the Father and coeternal.
claims: Hilary assigns eternity, form, and use to Father, Image, and Gift.
'Eternity' means the Father is from no one.

pll1d31c2-d1e3523.summary: Continues Augustine: the image, if it perfectly fills what it images, is equated to it, not the reverse. Hilary called it 'form' because of beauty: perfect congruence, first equality and likeness, supreme life and intellect, the perfect Word, and the art of the omnipotent wise God full of living, unchangeable reasons, in which God knows all he made.
claims: The Image is equated to its exemplar.
'Form' refers to the beauty and equality of the Image.
The Son is the art of God, full of the reasons of all things.

pll1d31c2-d1e3539.summary: Continues Augustine: the ineffable embrace of Father and Image is not without enjoyment, love, and joy; this delight or beatitude Hilary called 'use,' and it is the Holy Spirit, the sweetness of begetter and begotten, poured on all creatures according to their capacity. The three are determined by each other and infinite in themselves. Whoever sees this even in part should rejoice; whoever does not should strive by piety, not slander.
claims: 'Use' is the Holy Spirit, the delight of Father and Son.
The Spirit's sweetness is poured on all creatures.
The three are mutually determined and infinite.

pll1d31c2-d1e3563.summary: Comments that Hilary's words are so profound that even with Augustine's exposition they can hardly be understood, and the exposition itself is difficult and ambiguous.
claims: Hilary's text and Augustine's exposition remain difficult.

pll1d31c2-d1e3572.summary: Notes that in this exposition the three properties are not distinguished, but the hypostases are shown to be distinct; only 'eternity' seems to mark the property of innascibility. 'The image is equated to its original, not the reverse' means the Son has from the Father that he is equal, though Scripture calls each equal to the other.
claims: The exposition distinguishes hypostases, not properties.
'Eternity' marks innascibility.
The Son has his equality from the Father.

pll1d31c2-d1e3588.summary: Cites Hilary, De Synodis: the image is the undifferentiated form of the one it images; no one is his own image; an image is an undistinguished likeness equating one thing to another. So there is Father and Son, and the Son as Image must have in himself the form, nature, and essence of his author.
claims: No one is his own image.
The Son as Image has the nature and essence of the Father.

pll1d31c2-d1e3607.summary: Explains that Hilary assigned the propria of the persons by using relative personal names (Father, Image, Gift), which note distinguishing properties; Gift is relative as 'donum' is. But the three properties themselves are signified only by 'eternity,' meaning not paternity but the notion of being unbegotten.
claims: Father, Image, and Gift are relative personal names.
'Eternity' signifies innascibility, not paternity.

pll1d31c2-d1e3619.summary: Cites Hilary's anathema in De Synodis against calling the Son unbegotten and without beginning, as if there were two without principle and two gods. The Son is head of all, but God is head of the Son; innascibility belongs to one alone, so God is one; the Son is God because born of the unbegotten essence.
claims: Calling the Son unbegotten implies two gods.
Innascibility belongs to the Father alone.
The Son is God because born of the unbegotten essence.

pll1d31c2-d1e3640.summary: Further Hilary: God's will gave substance to all creatures, but perfect nativity from the impassible unborn substance gave nature to the Son. Creatures are such as God willed; the Son is such as God is, born of God's substance, having essence by origin, not by will as creatures do.
claims: Creatures have substance by God's will.
The Son has the divine nature by birth, not by will.

pll1d31c2-d1e3655.summary: Notes that Augustine, in De doctrina christiana I, shows the distinction of persons without expressing the three properties: unity in the Father, equality in the Son, concord of unity and equality in the Spirit; all one because of the Father, equal because of the Son, connected because of the Spirit. Each is God and full substance, all one God and substance; none is the others; they share one eternity, immutability, majesty, and power.
claims: Augustine assigns unity to the Father, equality to the Son, concord to the Spirit.
Each person is God; all are one God.
The three share one eternity, immutability, majesty, and power.

pl-l1d31c2.summary: Takes up Hilary's assignment of properties: 'eternity in the Father, form (species) in the Image, use (usus) in the Gift,' so difficult that Augustine labored over it. Augustine: 'eternity' means that the Father has no father from whom he is, while the Son is from the Father and coeternal; 'form' refers to the Image's beauty, perfect equality and likeness, supreme life and intellect, the Word and art of God full of living reasons; 'use' is the delight, love, and beatitude of Father and Image, the Holy Spirit, their sweetness poured on all creatures. Lombard admits the explanation remains difficult, notes that it distinguishes the hypostases rather than the three properties (except that 'eternity' marks innascibility), and explains how the Image is equated to the Father, with Hilary's further texts against two unbegottens. Augustine's De doctrina christiana assigns 'unity in the Father, equality in the Son, concord in the Spirit,' which also shows the distinction of persons.
claims: Hilary assigns eternity to the Father, form to the Image, and use to the Gift.
'Eternity' marks that the Father is from no one, i.e., innascibility.
'Form' refers to the beauty, equality, and likeness of the Image, the Word and art of God.
'Use' refers to the Spirit as the delight and love of Father and Image, poured on creatures.
The Image is equated to the Father, having its equality from the Father.
There cannot be two unbegotten; innascibility belongs to the Father alone.
Augustine assigns unity to the Father, equality to the Son, and concord to the Spirit.
